summary: Mark Bain's Memory Masterclass concludes its final segment with an extended Q&A and theoretical discussion. The security and privacy question—about sharing partial data in corporate or personal contexts—receives multiple answers. Mark suggests applying the right ontologies to enterprise cybersecurity stacks provides guardrails for navigating fuzziness and errors in access decisions. Daniel adds that all applications are built on Neo4j, which supports role-based access controls (RBAC) to prevent unauthorized data access. An audience member suggests isolating per-user personal graphs, which Mark and Daniel confirm works well in practice. Mark is then asked to revisit his earlier equations relating gravity, entropy, memory, compute, and I-squared. He restates two principles: memory times compute equals I-squared, and that attention, diffusion, and VAS (which perform smoothing) preserve asymmetries. He establishes the vocabulary: curvature equals attention equals gravity as the most important principle. He notes that diffusion, heat, and entropy are essentially the same thing, requiring tight definition alignment in forthcoming papers. Drawing on Perelman's work, he explains that bending spheres increases both entropy and curvature, and that Perelman's proof for 3D spheres implies there will be no other architectures for LLMs—only attention diffusion models and VAS-like structures that leave room for biases. The session closes with Mark thanking the guest speakers and audience, offering to answer further questions outside the room.

takeaways: Cognify builds semantic graphs on the fly from 30+ data sources with memory association layers inspired by cognitive science, supporting stateful temporal storage and agent-driven analysis

Neo4j's MCP memory server stores entities (name, type, observations) and relationships in a graph-native knowledge graph accessible across conversations and clients like Claude Desktop, Cursor IDE, and Windsurf
Graph databases as context layers provide rich context by identifying how entities relate, which is the core advantage over vector-only approaches
Daniel Chalef argues there is no one-size-fits-all memory; memory must be modeled after the business domain using explicit business objects defined via Pydantic, Zod, or Go structs
Mark's agentic firewall concept uses episodic/temporal memory in human-language shells to control code execution across terminals, machines, and sessions for enterprise security

GraphRAG Chat Arena is a prototype agentic memory simulation arena built with Google ADK, enabling cross-comparison of Mem0, Graphiti, Cognify, and Neo4j MCP solutions against a single Neo4j graph backend
Bad memory detection relies on noise, connectivity, and missing causal links—poorly connected nodes with high noise and absent causal relationships indicate incorrect or fuzzy memory
Neo4j supports role-based access controls (RBAC) for graph security, and per-user isolated personal graphs work well for privacy in enterprise contexts
Mark's theoretical framework equates curvature, attention, and gravity, and claims Perelman's 3D sphere proof implies attention diffusion models will remain the only LLM architectures
Mark believes MCPs are the future of agentic memory systems

sections.title: Workshop Introduction and Speaker Lineup
sections.summary: Mark introduces the workshop structure: a power talk, four live demos, a graph chat arena demonstration, and Q&A. Guest speakers Vasilia Marovitz (Cogni), Daniel Chalef (Graphiti/Zep), and Alex Gilmore (Neo4j) are announced. Audience is directed to join a Slack channel via QR code.

sections.title: Mark's Background and 2014 Stanford Conversations
sections.summary: Mark shares his math olympiad background and 2014 conversations at Stanford with Wojciech Zaremba and Ilya Sutskever, who were then at Google pitching an AI revolution. When he asked how AI systems would communicate, Ilya answered 'I don't know, I think they will invent their own language.'

sections.title: Theoretical Framework: Memory, Physics, and Graph Structure
sections.summary: Mark presents his conclusion that AI memory is any data in any format including code, algorithms, hardware, and causal changes. He draws parallels between LLM principles, neuroscience, and mathematics, referencing Perelman's work linking entropy with curvature. He proposes memory times compute approaches a squared imaginary unit circle ideal, and that scaling laws reduce biases toward zero.

sections.title: Causality, Hallucinations, and Agentic Systems
sections.summary: Mark argues hallucinations are necessary when memory or compute is insufficient for a problem's combinatorial space. Reasoning is reading asymmetries and causal links. Graph databases preserve causal relationships, distinguishing GraphRAG and enabling hallucination solutions. Agentic systems follow a network database principle requiring graph databases to recover causality.

sections.title: Vasilia's Cognify Demo: Developer Mexican Standoff
sections.summary: Vasilia demos Cognify ingesting GitHub data via API, building a semantic graph on the fly with an activity log. Agents read, write, and analyze using preconfigured weights and benchmarks. Cognify supports 30+ data sources, custom graphs from relational or semi-structured data, and memory association layers inspired by cognitive science. The stateful temporal aspect stores data back into the graph. The final hiring decision recommends the developer with a PhD in graphs.

sections.title: Alex Gilmore's Neo4j MCP Memory Server Demo
sections.summary: Alex demos Neo4j's memory MCP server using Claude Desktop and a Neo4j database (Aura cloud or local). A system prompt ensures recall and logging after each interaction. Entities have names, types, and observation lists; relationships identify how entities relate. The knowledge graph is visualized in Neo4j browser and can be reused across conversations and clients like Cursor IDE and Windsurf. Mark frames this as foundational agentic memory functionality.

sections.title: Daniel Chalef: Domain-Aware Memory and Temporal Graphs
sections.summary: Daniel (Graphiti/Zep, 10,000 GitHub stars) argues there is no one-size-fits-all memory and that memory must be modeled after the business domain. He demonstrates the problem with a media assistant that collects irrelevant facts (wake-up time, dog's name 'Melody') which pollute recall. Semantic similarity returns incorrect matches because vectors lack causal or relational structure. His key thesis: semantic similarity is not business relevance; the solution is domain-aware memory, not better semantic search. He begins a video demo due to Wi-Fi issues.

sections.title: Daniel's Zep Finance Coach Demo: Business Objects in Graph Memory
sections.summary: Daniel demos a Zep-powered finance coach application that stores explicit business objects—financial goals, debts, income sources—defined by developers using Pydantic, Zod, or Go structs with field-level business rules. A TypeScript financial goal schema using Zep's SDK defines entity types, descriptions, and fields. Tools run multiple concurrent Zep searches filtered by node type. When the user mentions $5,000/month rent, Zep captures it and creates a debt account entity in the knowledge graph with developer-defined fields. Daniel references a paper explaining the approach. Mark confirms Slack access for the audience before transitioning.

sections.title: Mark's Agentic Firewall Use Case
sections.summary: Mark presents his cybersecurity lab background, describing a project requiring navigation between 27-29 different terminals and shells with proprietary languages. He realized LLMs can translate these languages and create a 'human language shell' that excels with episodic/temporal memory of shell history. He demos natural-language commands (pwd, docker ps, Apache status, recalling prior commands). He argues temporal and episodic logs spanning all users, machines, and sessions provide strong security context. He believes enterprise agents executing code in terminals will go through agentic firewalls.

sections.title: GraphRAG Chat Arena Demo
sections.summary: Mark introduces the GraphRAG Chat Arena, a prototype 'agentic memory arena' like web arena but for memory, built with Google ADK. Created with Jeru from Namal Index, the repo contains integrations for Mem0, Graphiti, and Cognify, testable via both libraries and MCPs. Users switch between agents (Neo4j agent, Cypher graph agent) in a chat interface. All technologies run against a single Neo4j graph backend. Users can add data through one solution (e.g., Cypher) and search through another (e.g., Graphiti), enabling cross-solution comparison of graph creation and retrieval.

sections.title: Q&A: Bad Memory, Causal Links, Security, and Theoretical Equations
sections.summary: A brief Q&A begins. Lucas asks how to decide what constitutes bad memory over time. Mark answers scientifically: noisy, less connected nodes are potentially incorrect; decrease noise via redundancy and relationships. Daniel adds a practical approach using Pydantic modeling with weights on edges and nodes, temporal weighting, and custom logic. Mark adds that missing causal links indicate fuzziness. On security and privacy, Mark suggests applying the right ontologies to enterprise cybersecurity stacks as guardrails. Daniel notes all applications run on Neo4j, which supports role-based access controls. An audience member suggests isolating per-user personal graphs, which works well in practice. Mark then revisits his earlier equations at an audience member's request: memory times compute equals I-squared, and attention/diffusion/VAS preserve asymmetries. He explains curvature equals attention equals gravity as the core principle, that diffusion, heat, and entropy are essentially the same phenomenon, and that Perelman's proof about bending 3D spheres implies attention diffusion models will remain the only LLM architectures. The session closes with thanks to guest speakers and the audience.
